question: Which provision of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 codifies the principle of Joint Liability based on Common Intention (Section 34 IPC)?
options: Section 3(5)
Section 190
Section 61
Section 111
explanation: Section 3(5) BNS replaces Section 34 IPC: when a criminal act is done by several persons in furtherance of the common intention of all, each is liable as if done by him alone.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; Section 3(5) BNS corresponds to Section 34 IPC.
optionBreakdown.B: Section 190 BNS is common object (S. 149 IPC).

learningObjective: Identify BNS provision for Common Intention.

question: Does Section 3(5) BNS / Section 34 IPC create a distinct, standalone substantive offence?
options: Yes, it is punishable with 7 years imprisonment
No; it is a rule of evidence and principle of joint liability, not a substantive offence
Yes, in murder cases only
Yes, when 5 or more persons participate
explanation: Section 34 IPC / Section 3(5) BNS does not create any new offence; it lays down a principle of joint vicarious liability attributing acts done in furtherance of common intention.

optionBreakdown.A: No separate sentence exists for S. 34.
optionBreakdown.B: Correct; it is a rule of joint liability, not a distinct offence.

learningObjective: Understand the nature of Common Intention.

question: In the landmark 'Indus River Case' (Mahbub Shah v. King-Emperor, 1945), the Privy Council established the crucial distinction between:
options: Motive and intention
Common intention and similar intention
Preparation and attempt
Manslaughter and murder
explanation: Sir Madhavan Nair drew the classic line: common intention implies a pre-arranged plan and prior meeting of minds; similar intention arises independently without pre-concert.

optionBreakdown.A: Different legal concepts.
optionBreakdown.B: Correct; common intention requires pre-concert; similar intention does not.

learningObjective: Distinguish common intention from similar intention.

question: In the famous 'Post Office Case' (Barendra Kumar Ghosh v. King-Emperor, 1925), Lord Sumner used which immortal phrase to hold the guard liable for murder?
options: The hand that strikes is the hand of all
They also serve who only stand and wait
He who plans the deed executes the deed
Silence is consent in murder
explanation: Lord Sumner quoted Milton's phrase: 'They also serve who only stand and wait', holding that the person standing outside to warn of danger actively participated in furtherance of common intention.

optionBreakdown.A: Informal paraphrase.
optionBreakdown.B: Correct; 'They also serve who only stand and wait'.

learningObjective: Master Barendra Kumar Ghosh participation doctrine.

question: Can common intention develop on the spot during the course of the transaction without prior long-term conspiracy?
options: No, it requires days of written planning
Yes; common intention can develop on the spur of the moment during the commission of the offence
Only if approved by a gang leader
Only in riot cases
explanation: In Kripal Singh v. State of U.P. and Pandurang v. State of Hyderabad, the Supreme Court held that common intention can develop instantaneously on the spot.

optionBreakdown.A: Prior meeting need not be long-term.
optionBreakdown.B: Correct; can develop on the spot.

provision: Pandurang v. State of Hyderabad, AIR 1955 SC 216
learningObjective: Understand instantaneous development of common intention.

question: What is the minimum number of persons required to attract Section 3(5) BNS / Section 34 IPC?
options: One person
Two persons
Five persons
Seven persons
explanation: The statutory words are 'done by several persons', which requires a minimum of at least two persons acting together.

optionBreakdown.A: Cannot have common intention alone.
optionBreakdown.B: Correct; minimum two persons.

learningObjective: Recall minimum number for common intention.

question: A and B go together armed with knives to rob C. A stands outside the room holding a knife to prevent anyone from entering, while B stabs C to death inside. A is liable for murder under:
options: Section 103 read with Section 3(5) BNS
Section 105 BNS only
Simple hurt only
No liability as A did not stab C
explanation: Under Barendra Kumar Ghosh and Section 3(5) BNS, physical participation by guarding the door in furtherance of the pre-concerted robbery and violence makes A jointly liable for murder.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; joint liability for murder under S. 103 r/w S. 3(5).
optionBreakdown.B: Not reduced to culpable homicide.
optionBreakdown.D: Physical presence and guarding constitutes active participation.

learningObjective: Apply common intention to guarding accomplice.

question: What is the essential element that distinguishes Section 3(5) BNS / Section 34 IPC from Section 190 BNS / Section 149 IPC?
options: Section 34 requires active participation; Section 149 requires mere membership of an unlawful assembly
Section 34 requires 5 persons; Section 149 requires 2
Section 34 is a distinct offence; Section 149 is not
Section 34 applies only to property offences
explanation: Section 34 requires pre-concert and participation in the criminal act; Section 149 requires membership of an unlawful assembly (5+ persons) with a common object, without requiring individual participation in the fatal blow.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; active participation vs mere assembly membership.
optionBreakdown.B: Reversed numbers.
optionBreakdown.C: Section 149 creates a distinct offence; Section 34 does not.

provision: Nanak Chand v. State of Punjab, AIR 1955 SC 274
learningObjective: Contrast Section 34 and Section 149.

question: In Suresh v. State of U.P. (2001), the Supreme Court affirmed that participation under Section 34 IPC / Section 3(5) BNS:
options: Always requires overt physical assault
Can be physical, or by moral support, keeping watch, or giving signals, provided there is shared common intention
Requires firing of a weapon
Is irrelevant if conspiracy is proved
explanation: Participation need not be violent assault; standing guard, giving signals, or keeping watch in furtherance of the common design constitutes sufficient participation.

optionBreakdown.A: Overt violent act not strictly necessary.
optionBreakdown.B: Correct; non-physical or guarding participation suffices.
optionBreakdown.D: Participation is the core of Section 34.

learningObjective: Master modes of participation under Section 34 / 3(5).

question: If four persons are charged under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC / Section 3(5) BNS, and three are acquitted due to lack of evidence, can the sole remaining accused be convicted with the aid of Section 34 / 3(5)?
options: Yes, an individual can have common intention alone
No, unless it is proved that the sole accused acted jointly with some other unidentified or named persons who shared the common intention
Yes, automatically
No, the sole accused must be acquitted of all charges
explanation: Under settled law, an individual cannot be convicted with the aid of Section 34 alone, unless evidence shows they acted with other persons (even if unidentified).

optionBreakdown.A: Single person cannot have joint liability alone.
optionBreakdown.B: Correct; requires proof of other participants.
optionBreakdown.D: Can be convicted substantively for his own acts.

provision: Prabhu Babaji v. State of Bombay, AIR 1956 SC 51
learningObjective: Analyze effect of acquittal of co-accused in Section 34.

question: Under Section 189 BNS / Section 141 IPC, an assembly of persons is designated an 'Unlawful Assembly' if it consists of at least:
options: Three persons
Five persons
Seven persons
Ten persons
explanation: Section 189 BNS / Section 141 IPC strictly requires an assembly of five (5) or more persons having one of the five specified common objects.

optionBreakdown.A: Three is insufficient.
optionBreakdown.B: Correct; minimum five persons.

learningObjective: Recall minimum membership of unlawful assembly.

question: Which of the following is NOT one of the five statutory common objects specified in Section 189 BNS / Section 141 IPC?
options: To overawe by criminal force the Central or State Government or Parliament
To resist the execution of any law or of any legal process
To commit any mischief or criminal trespass or other offence
To hold a peaceful silent prayer gathering in a private home
explanation: Section 189 BNS / Section 141 IPC specifies 5 unlawful objects: overawing government, resisting legal process, committing offence/mischief/trespass, enforcing right by criminal force, and compelling illegal acts.

optionBreakdown.A: Statutory object (First).
optionBreakdown.B: Statutory object (Second).
optionBreakdown.D: Correct; peaceful private prayer is not an unlawful object.

learningObjective: Identify statutory common objects.

question: Which provision of BNS 2023 replaces Section 149 IPC concerning every member of an unlawful assembly guilty of offence committed in prosecution of common object?
options: Section 3(5)
Section 190
Section 191
Section 194
explanation: Section 190 BNS corresponds directly to Section 149 IPC (constructive joint liability of unlawful assembly members).

optionBreakdown.A: Section 3(5) is S. 34 IPC.
optionBreakdown.B: Correct; Section 190 BNS is S. 149 IPC.

learningObjective: Map BNS Section 190 to IPC Section 149.

question: What is the crucial two-fold test for constructive liability under Section 190 BNS / Section 149 IPC?
options: Act was done in prosecution of the common object, OR was such as the members knew to be likely to be committed in prosecution of that object
Act was planned 24 hours in advance
All members used deadly firearms
Act was committed in daylight
explanation: Section 190 BNS / Section 149 IPC has two limbs: (1) offence committed in prosecution of common object; or (2) offence which members knew was likely to be committed.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; two statutory limbs of Section 149/190.
optionBreakdown.B: Pre-planning not required.

learningObjective: Master the two limbs of Section 149 constructive liability.

question: In Mizaji v. State of U.P. (1959), the Supreme Court interpreted the second limb of Section 149 IPC ('knew to be likely') to mean:
options: Mere possibility of crime
Knowledge that the offence was likely to be committed, which is more than a mere possibility and implies real foresight
Certainty that murder will occur
Prior agreement in writing
explanation: The Supreme Court held that 'knew' means something more than a speculation or possibility; it implies a state of mind where members foresee the offence as a likely incident.

optionBreakdown.A: Mere possibility insufficient.
optionBreakdown.B: Correct; real foresight of likelihood.

learningObjective: Apply Mizaji doctrine on knowledge of likelihood.

question: What happens when six persons are charged under Section 302 read with Section 149 IPC / Section 190 BNS, and two are acquitted, leaving four persons convicted?
options: The four can still be convicted under Section 149 without any qualifications
Conviction under Section 149 cannot stand unless it is proved that there were other unidentified persons making the total at least five
All four must be discharged immediately
The offence becomes dacoity
explanation: In Ram Bilas Singh v. State of Bihar, the Supreme Court held that Section 149 requires at least 5 persons; if acquittals reduce the number below 5, S. 149 fails unless others participated.

optionBreakdown.A: Four persons cannot constitute unlawful assembly.
optionBreakdown.B: Correct; requires proof that total assembly was 5+.
optionBreakdown.C: Can be convicted individually or under S. 34 if common intention proved.

learningObjective: Analyze effect of reducing assembly below five persons.

question: Under Section 191 BNS / Section 146 IPC, 'Rioting' is defined as:
options: Whenever force or violence is used by an unlawful assembly, or by any member thereof, in prosecution of the common object
Whenever five persons speak loudly on a public road
Whenever two persons fight in a cinema hall
Whenever traffic is blocked by vehicles
explanation: Section 191 BNS / Section 146 IPC defines rioting: an unlawful assembly using force or violence in prosecution of common object.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; force/violence by unlawful assembly.
optionBreakdown.B: Loud speech is not rioting.
optionBreakdown.C: Two persons fighting in public is Affray under S. 194 BNS / S. 159 IPC.

learningObjective: Define Rioting under BNS.

question: Under Section 194 BNS / Section 159 IPC, 'Affray' requires:
options: Five persons using deadly weapons
Two or more persons, by fighting in a public place, disturbing the public peace
Damage to private property exceeding Rs 10,000
Assembly in a private drawing room
explanation: Section 194 BNS / Section 159 IPC defines Affray: when two or more persons, by fighting in a public place, disturb the public peace.

optionBreakdown.A: This is rioting/dacoity.
optionBreakdown.B: Correct; 2+ persons fighting in public place disturbing peace.

learningObjective: Define Affray in criminal law.

question: What is the punishment for committing an Affray under Section 194(2) BNS / Section 160 IPC?
options: Imprisonment up to 1 month, or fine up to Rs 1,000, or both
Rigorous imprisonment up to 3 years
Life imprisonment
Community service for 1 year
explanation: Affray is a petty offence punished with imprisonment extending up to one month, or fine up to Rs 1,000, or both.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; max 1 month or fine.
optionBreakdown.B: Too severe.

learningObjective: Recall punishment for Affray.

question: Can an assembly which was lawful when it assembled subsequently become an unlawful assembly?
options: No, character is fixed at the time of gathering
Yes; under Section 189 Explanation BNS / Section 141 Explanation IPC, an assembly which was not unlawful when it assembled, may subsequently become an unlawful assembly
Only if police declare it so under Section 144 CrPC
Only after sunset
explanation: The statutory explanation explicitly provides: 'An assembly which was not unlawful when it assembled, may subsequently become an unlawful assembly.'

optionBreakdown.A: Assembly can change character.
optionBreakdown.B: Correct; lawful assembly can turn unlawful.

provision: BNS Section 189 Explanation / IPC S. 141 Exp.
learningObjective: Understand evolution of lawful into unlawful assembly.

question: Under Section 45 BNS / Section 107 IPC, in how many statutory ways can a person abet the doing of a thing?
options: Two ways
Three ways
Four ways
Five ways
explanation: Section 45 BNS / Section 107 IPC specifies three ways of abetment: (1) Instigation; (2) Conspiracy; (3) Intentional aid.

optionBreakdown.A: Two is incomplete.
optionBreakdown.B: Correct; Instigation, Conspiracy, and Aiding.

learningObjective: Identify the three statutory modes of abetment.

question: A public officer is authorized by warrant from a Court of Justice to apprehend Z. B, knowing that fact and also that C is not Z, wilfully represents to the officer that C is Z, and thereby intentionally causes the apprehension of C. B abets the arrest by:
options: Conspiracy
Instigation under Section 45 Explanation 1 BNS
Passive silence
Duress
explanation: Explanation 1 to Section 107 IPC / Section 45 BNS provides that wilful misrepresentation causing an act constitutes abetment by instigation.

optionBreakdown.A: No agreement between B and officer.
optionBreakdown.B: Correct; instigation by wilful misrepresentation.

learningObjective: Apply instigation by wilful misrepresentation.

question: Can a person be guilty of abetting the abetment of an offence under Section 47 BNS / Section 108 Explanation 4 IPC?
options: No, abetment cannot be compounded
Yes; the abetment of an abetment of an offence is itself an offence
Only if the main offence is murder
Only if the second abettor is present on the spot
explanation: Explanation 4 to Section 108 IPC / Section 47 BNS explicitly enacts: 'The abetment of an abetment of an offence is an offence.' (e.g. A instigates B to instigate C to murder Z).

optionBreakdown.A: Statute permits it.
optionBreakdown.B: Correct; abetment of abetment is an offence.

learningObjective: Understand abetment of an abetment.

question: A instigates B to murder C. B refuses to do so. What offence has A committed?
options: No offence because the act was not committed
Abetment of murder under Section 46 BNS / Section 108 IPC
Attempt to murder
Criminal intimidation only
explanation: Under Explanation 2 to Section 108 IPC / Section 46 BNS, to constitute abetment, it is NOT necessary that the act abetted should be committed or that the effect should be caused.

optionBreakdown.A: Abetment is complete upon instigation.
optionBreakdown.B: Correct; abetment is an inchoate offence complete upon instigation.

learningObjective: Master the inchoate nature of abetment.

question: A instigates a child of six years to set fire to a dwelling house. The child does not understand the nature of the act and sets fire. A is guilty of:
options: No offence because the child is doli incapax
Abetment of mischief by fire, punishable as if the child were capable of committing the offence
Only negligence
Contempt of court
explanation: Under Explanation 3 to Section 108 IPC / Section 46 BNS, it is not necessary that the person abetted should be capable by law of committing an offence. The abettor is fully liable.

optionBreakdown.A: Child's incapacity does not protect abettor.
optionBreakdown.B: Correct; abettor is liable though actor is legally immune.

learningObjective: Apply abetment of person incapable of committing crime.

question: Under Section 50 BNS / Section 111 IPC, an abettor is liable for a different act committed by the person abetted IF:
options: The act done was a probable consequence of the abetment, and was committed under the influence of the instigation
The abettor was related to the actor
The actor used the abettor's car
The victim was a public servant
explanation: Under Section 50 BNS / Section 111 IPC (Doctrine of Probable Consequence), the abettor is liable for a different act if it was a probable consequence of the abetment.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; probable consequence doctrine.
optionBreakdown.B: Kinship irrelevant.

learningObjective: Master the probable consequence doctrine in abetment.

question: A instigates B to burn Z's house. B sets fire to the house and at the same time commits theft of property there. Is A liable for the theft?
options: Yes, A instigated B
No, because the theft was not a probable consequence of burning the house
Yes, under joint liability
Yes, if A accepted a share of the stolen property
explanation: Under Illustration (a) to Section 111 IPC / Section 50 BNS, A is guilty of abetting the burning of the house, but is not guilty of abetting the theft, for the theft was a distinct act and not a probable consequence of the burning.

optionBreakdown.A: Overstates liability.
optionBreakdown.B: Correct; theft is distinct, not a probable consequence of burning.
optionBreakdown.D: Receiving stolen property is separate S. 317.

learningObjective: Apply Section 111 probable consequence illustration.

question: Under Section 52 BNS / Section 113 IPC, when an act is abetted and a different effect is caused, the abettor is liable for the effect caused if:
options: The abettor knew that the act abetted was likely to cause that effect
The victim was elderly
The offence took place at night
The weapon was licensed
explanation: Section 52 BNS / Section 113 IPC provides that the abettor is liable for the different effect caused in the same manner as if he had directly intended it, if he knew the act was likely to cause that effect.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; foresight of likelihood of effect.
optionBreakdown.B: Age irrelevant.

learningObjective: Understand different effect liability in abetment.

question: What is the consequence under Section 53 BNS / Section 114 IPC when an abettor who would be punishable is present when the act is committed?
options: He is treated as an accessory after the fact
He shall be deemed to have committed such act or offence himself
He gets half the punishment
He is acquitted
explanation: Section 53 BNS / Section 114 IPC creates a statutory fiction: whenever an abettor is present when the act is committed, he shall be deemed to have committed the offence himself.

optionBreakdown.A: Not accessory.
optionBreakdown.B: Correct; deemed to have committed offence himself.

learningObjective: Recall deemed principal rule in abetment presence.

question: A gives poison to B with instructions to administer it to C. B takes the poison to C's house, but throws it in the river instead. What is A's liability?
options: A has committed no offence because no poison was given to C
A is guilty of abetment of murder
A is guilty of simple hurt
A is guilty of nuisance
explanation: Abetment is an independent inchoate offence; instigation and providing poison completes the abetment of murder regardless of B's subsequent abandonment.

optionBreakdown.A: Abetment does not depend on commission.
optionBreakdown.B: Correct; abetment of murder complete.

learningObjective: Apply inchoate nature of abetment to abandoned crime.

question: Which provision of BNS 2023 replaces Sections 120A and 120B of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 for Criminal Conspiracy?
options: Section 3(5)
Section 61
Section 111
Section 189
explanation: Section 61 BNS consolidates the definition (S. 120A) and punishment (S. 120B) of Criminal Conspiracy into a single section.

optionBreakdown.A: Section 3(5) is S. 34 IPC.
optionBreakdown.B: Correct; Section 61 BNS is Criminal Conspiracy.

learningObjective: Map BNS Section 61 for Criminal Conspiracy.

question: Under Section 61(1) BNS / Section 120A IPC, when two or more persons agree to do an ILLEGAL ACT (which is an offence), is an overt act necessary to complete the conspiracy?
options: Yes, an overt act must always be proved
No; bare agreement itself constitutes the offence of criminal conspiracy without any overt act
Yes, money must be exchanged
Yes, weapon must be procured
explanation: The proviso to Section 120A IPC / Section 61(1) BNS provides that no overt act is necessary where the agreement is to commit an offence; the bare agreement itself is the crime.

optionBreakdown.A: Overt act needed only if act is not an offence.
optionBreakdown.B: Correct; bare agreement to commit an offence is complete conspiracy.

learningObjective: Master agreement as the gist of conspiracy.

question: When is an OVERT ACT required to constitute criminal conspiracy under Section 61(1) BNS / Section 120A IPC?
options: When the agreement is to commit murder
When the agreement is to do an act which is not an offence, but is an illegal act or an act by illegal means
When the conspirators are more than ten
In cyber-crimes only
explanation: The proviso stipulates: 'Provided that no agreement except an agreement to commit an offence shall amount to a criminal conspiracy unless some act besides the agreement is done...'.

optionBreakdown.A: Offences need no overt act.
optionBreakdown.B: Correct; non-offence illegal acts require an overt act.
optionBreakdown.C: Number of conspirators doesn't change rule.

learningObjective: Distinguish offence conspiracy from non-offence illegal conspiracy.

question: In State (NCT of Delhi) v. Navjot Sandhu (Parliament Attack Case, 2005), the Supreme Court affirmed that criminal conspiracy is:
options: A substantive offence that is continuous in nature from the time of agreement until completion or abandonment
A minor misdemeanour requiring proof by eyewitnesses of the secret meeting
Admissible only if written minutes exist
Punishable only if treason is committed
explanation: The Supreme Court held conspiracy is a continuing offence hatched in secrecy; direct evidence is rarely available and agreement is inferred from circumstantial acts.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; continuing substantive offence.
optionBreakdown.B: Not minor; secret meetings rarely have direct witnesses.

learningObjective: Apply Navjot Sandhu criminal conspiracy doctrine.

question: What is the punishment for criminal conspiracy to commit an offence punishable with death, life imprisonment, or rigorous imprisonment for 2+ years under S. 61(2) BNS / S. 120B(1) IPC?
options: Simple imprisonment up to 6 months
Punished in the same manner as if he had abetted such offence
Fine of Rs 5,000 only
Community service
explanation: Section 61(2)(a) BNS / Section 120B(1) IPC provides that the conspirator shall be punished in the same manner as if he had abetted such offence.

optionBreakdown.A: 6 months is for minor offences under clause (b).
optionBreakdown.B: Correct; punished as an abettor of the offence.

learningObjective: Recall penalty for serious criminal conspiracies.

question: What is the minimum number of persons required to form a criminal conspiracy under Section 61 BNS / Section 120A IPC?
options: One person
Two persons
Three persons
Five persons
explanation: A person cannot conspire with himself; Section 61 BNS / Section 120A IPC explicitly requires 'two or more persons'.

optionBreakdown.A: Conspiracy requires agreement between two or more.
optionBreakdown.B: Correct; minimum two persons.

learningObjective: Recall minimum membership for conspiracy.

question: In Topandas v. State of Bombay (1955), four persons were charged with criminal conspiracy. Three were acquitted on trial. Can the conviction of the sole fourth accused for conspiracy stand?
options: Yes, if he was the mastermind
No; one person alone cannot be convicted of criminal conspiracy when all other alleged conspirators have been acquitted
Yes, if he confesses
Yes, on payment of fine
explanation: The Supreme Court held that it is an established principle of law that one person cannot be convicted of conspiracy where all co-accused have been acquitted, as an agreement requires at least two minds.

optionBreakdown.A: Cannot agree with oneself.
optionBreakdown.B: Correct; sole accused cannot be convicted of conspiracy.

learningObjective: Apply Topandas acquittal of co-conspirators rule.

question: Is it necessary that every conspirator must actively participate in every single act done in execution of the conspiracy?
options: Yes, all conspirators must be physically present at all acts
No; once common design is established, every conspirator is liable for acts done by any co-conspirator in execution of the common plan
Only the conspirator who supplied weapons is liable
Only the person who struck the fatal blow is liable
explanation: In Yash Pal Mittal v. State of Punjab, the Supreme Court confirmed that it is not necessary that each conspirator must know every detail or participate in every stage.

optionBreakdown.A: Presence not required.
optionBreakdown.B: Correct; agency principle binds all conspirators.
optionBreakdown.D: Fatal striker is not sole liable person.

learningObjective: Master agency liability in criminal conspiracy.

question: What is the punishment for criminal conspiracy to commit an offence NOT punishable with death, life, or 2+ years under S. 61(2)(b) BNS / S. 120B(2) IPC?
options: Imprisonment up to six (6) months, or fine, or both
Imprisonment up to 2 years
Life imprisonment
Community service for 2 years
explanation: Under Section 61(2)(b) BNS / Section 120B(2) IPC, conspiracy for minor offences is punishable with imprisonment up to six months, or fine, or both.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; up to six months or fine or both.
optionBreakdown.B: Incorrect.

learningObjective: Recall penalty for minor conspiracies.

question: How does Criminal Conspiracy under Section 61 BNS differ from Abetment by Conspiracy under Section 45(Secondly) BNS?
options: Section 61 requires an overt act; Section 45 does not
In Section 61 bare agreement to commit offence is punishable; in Section 45 abetment, an act or illegal omission must take place in pursuance of the conspiracy
Section 61 applies only to public servants
Section 45 is a civil wrong
explanation: In Pramatha Nath Talukdar v. Saroj Ranjan Sarkar, the Supreme Court held: under Section 107/45 abetment by conspiracy, an act or illegal omission must occur in pursuance; under Section 120A/61, bare agreement to commit an offence is substantive crime.

optionBreakdown.A: Inverts the rule.
optionBreakdown.B: Correct; Section 61 bare agreement vs Section 45 overt act in pursuance.

learningObjective: Distinguish substantive conspiracy from abetment by conspiracy.

question: Which provisions of BNS 2023 define and punish Culpable Homicide and Murder?
options: Section 100 defines Culpable Homicide; Section 101 defines Murder; Section 103 punishes Murder
Section 103 defines Culpable Homicide; Section 105 defines Murder
Section 299 and 300 (unchanged numbers)
Section 302 defines Culpable Homicide; Section 304 punishes Murder
explanation: In BNS 2023: Section 100 defines Culpable Homicide (IPC 299); Section 101 defines Murder (IPC 300); Section 103 punishes Murder (IPC 302); Section 105 punishes Culpable Homicide (IPC 304).

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; Section 100 (CH) and Section 101 (Murder).
optionBreakdown.B: Incorrect mapping.
optionBreakdown.C: Numbers are completely restructured in BNS.

learningObjective: Map BNS homicide provisions.

question: The classic legal formula establishing that 'all murders are culpable homicide, but all culpable homicides are not murder' was authored by Melvill J. in which landmark decision?
options: Reg. v. Govinda (1876)
K.M. Nanavati v. State of Maharashtra
Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab
MacDonald v. State
explanation: In Reg. v. Govinda (1876) ILR 1 Bom 147, Melvill J. drew the comparative tabular distinction between Section 299 and Section 300 IPC based on degrees of probability.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; Reg. v. Govinda (1876).
optionBreakdown.B: Nanavati is provocation.
optionBreakdown.C: Bachan Singh is rarest of rare death penalty.

learningObjective: Identify Reg. v. Govinda formula.

question: What is the critical distinction between Section 100(b) BNS / Section 299(b) IPC and Section 101(c) BNS / Section 300(3) IPC?
options: Section 299(b) requires 'likely to cause death'; Section 300(3) requires 'sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death'
Section 299(b) applies to poisons only
Section 300(3) requires weapon registration
Section 299(b) is civil; Section 300(3) is criminal
explanation: Melvill J. in Govinda showed: Section 299(b) requires bodily injury 'likely to cause death' (lower probability); Section 300(3) requires bodily injury 'sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death' (high probability/virtual certainty).

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; 'likely' vs 'sufficient in ordinary course of nature'.
optionBreakdown.B: Applies across all weapons.

learningObjective: Master probability distinction between 299(b) and 300(3).

question: In Virsa Singh v. State of Punjab (1958), Vivian Bose J. formulated the definitive four-step test for Section 300(3) IPC / Section 101(c) BNS, holding that:
options: Prosecution must prove the accused intended to cause death specifically
Prosecution must prove an intentional bodily injury was inflicted, and that injury objectively was sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death
The doctor must testify that death was accidental
The accused must have used a licensed firearm
explanation: Vivian Bose J. held: it is not necessary to prove intention to cause death; it is enough to prove that the accused intended to inflict that particular bodily injury, and that injury was objectively sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death.

optionBreakdown.A: Intention to kill is 300(1), not 300(3).
optionBreakdown.B: Correct; Virsa Singh classic four-point test.

provision: Virsa Singh v. State of Punjab, AIR 1958 SC 465
learningObjective: Master Virsa Singh Section 300(3) test.

question: Under Section 101(d) BNS / Section 300(4) IPC (imminently dangerous act), which element distinguishes it from Section 100(c) BNS / Section 299(c) IPC?
options: Act is so imminently dangerous that it must in all probability cause death without any excuse
Act is committed in a private house
Act causes financial loss
Act is committed by multiple persons
explanation: Section 300(4) requires an act so imminently dangerous that it must in all probability cause death, committed without any excuse for incurring the risk (e.g. firing a cannon into a crowded street).

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; imminently dangerous act without excuse.
optionBreakdown.B: Location irrelevant.

learningObjective: Analyze Section 300(4) imminently dangerous act.

question: A, knowing that B is labouring under an enlarged spleen so that a blow is likely to kill him, strikes B a single moderate blow on the abdomen, rupturing the spleen and killing him. A ordinary blow would not kill a healthy man. A is guilty of:
options: Murder under Section 101(b) BNS / Section 300(2) IPC
Simple hurt only under Section 115 BNS
Grievous hurt only
No offence under accident
explanation: Under Section 300(2) IPC / Section 101(b) BNS (Illustration b), if the offender knows the special physical condition of the victim and intends to cause bodily injury likely to cause death to that particular person, it is Murder.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; special knowledge of physical infirmity makes it Murder.
optionBreakdown.B: Hurt is eclipsed by fatal result with knowledge.

learningObjective: Apply special victim knowledge in Section 300(2).

question: Under Explanation 1 to Section 100 BNS / Section 299 IPC, if a person causes bodily injury to another who is labouring under a disease or disorder, and thereby accelerates death, the person:
options: Is guilty of simple hurt only
Shall be deemed to have caused his death
Is exempt from homicide liability
Is liable only for medical expenses
explanation: Explanation 1 to Section 299 IPC / Section 100 BNS explicitly provides: 'A person who causes bodily injury to another who is labouring under a disorder, disease or bodily infirmity, and thereby accelerates the death of that other, shall be deemed to have caused his death.'

optionBreakdown.A: Homicide liability applies.
optionBreakdown.B: Correct; deemed to have caused death by acceleration.

learningObjective: Recall acceleration of death rule in culpable homicide.

question: Under Explanation 3 to Section 100 BNS / Section 299 IPC, causing the death of a child in the mother's womb is:
options: Murder
Culpable homicide
Not culpable homicide, though causing death after any part of the child has been brought forth, even if not fully breathed, is culpable homicide
Attempt to commit suicide
explanation: Explanation 3 provides that causing death of child in womb is not culpable homicide; but it may amount to culpable homicide if any part has been brought forth, though child may not have breathed.

optionBreakdown.A: Fetus in womb is S. 91 BNS / S. 312-315 IPC.
optionBreakdown.B: Not culpable homicide while entirely in womb.

learningObjective: Distinguish fetal death from culpable homicide.

question: A intentionally aims a rifle at B intending to kill him, but misses and shoots C dead, whom A never saw. Under Section 102 BNS / Section 301 IPC (Doctrine of Transferred Malice), A is guilty of:
options: Culpable homicide not amounting to murder
Murder of C, of the same description as if he had killed B
Negligent homicide under Section 106 BNS
Accident
explanation: Under Section 301 IPC / Section 102 BNS (Doctrine of Transferred Malice / Aberratio Ictus), the culpability for killing C is identical to the intention entertained towards B.

optionBreakdown.A: Not reduced to culpable homicide.
optionBreakdown.B: Correct; transferred malice treats death of C as murder.

learningObjective: Apply Doctrine of Transferred Malice.

question: What is the mandatory punishment for Murder under Section 103(1) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023?
options: Death or imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine
Imprisonment for 10 years and fine
Death penalty mandatorily in all cases
Community service for 5 years
explanation: Section 103(1) BNS provides that whoever commits murder shall be punished with death or imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; death or life imprisonment, and fine.
optionBreakdown.B: 10 years is for culpable homicide Part II.
optionBreakdown.C: Mandatory death penalty was struck down in Mithu v. State of Punjab.

learningObjective: Recall statutory penalties for Murder.

question: Which landmark Supreme Court decision laid down the authoritative test for Grave and Sudden Provocation under Exception 1 to Murder?
options: K.M. Nanavati v. State of Maharashtra (1962)
Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab (1980)
Machhi Singh v. State of Punjab (1983)
Kehar Singh v. State (Delhi Admn.) (1988)
explanation: K.M. Nanavati v. State of Maharashtra (AIR 1962 SC 605) formulated the principles of grave and sudden provocation, cooling time, and the reasonable person test.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; K.M. Nanavati is the locus classicus on Exception 1.
optionBreakdown.B: Deals with rarest of rare doctrine for death penalty.
optionBreakdown.C: Deals with sentencing guidelines in murder.

provision: BNS S. 101 Exception 1 / IPC S. 300 Exception 1
learningObjective: Master Grave and Sudden Provocation doctrine.

question: How many statutory exceptions to Murder reduce culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 101(1) BNS (Section 300 IPC)?
options: 3 exceptions
4 exceptions
5 exceptions
7 exceptions
explanation: Both IPC Section 300 and BNS Section 101 contain exactly 5 statutory exceptions.

optionBreakdown.A: Incorrect; there are 5 exceptions.
optionBreakdown.B: Incorrect.

learningObjective: Recall number of murder exceptions.

question: Exception 2 to Section 101 BNS (Section 300 IPC) applies when the offender causes death while:
options: Acting in sudden fight without premeditation
Exceeding the right of private defence in good faith without premeditation
Being a public servant exceeding lawful powers
Causing death with the consent of a person above 18 years
explanation: Exception 2 applies when culpable homicide is committed in good faith exceeding the right of private defence without intention of doing more harm than necessary.

optionBreakdown.A: This is Exception 4 (sudden fight).
optionBreakdown.B: Correct; Exception 2 covers exceeding private defence in good faith.
optionBreakdown.D: This is Exception 5 (consent of adult victim).

provision: BNS S. 101 Exception 2 / IPC S. 300 Exception 2
learningObjective: Distinguish Exception 2 from other exceptions.

question: For Exception 4 (Sudden Fight) to apply, which of the following conditions is NOT required?
options: Sudden fight without premeditation
Sudden quarrel and heat of passion
Offender must not have taken undue advantage or acted in a cruel manner
Provocation must have been given by the victim prior to the fight
explanation: In Exception 4, it is immaterial which party offers the provocation or commits the first assault; prior provocation by victim is not a prerequisite.

optionBreakdown.A: Required statutory condition.
optionBreakdown.B: Required statutory condition.
optionBreakdown.D: Correct; explanation to Exception 4 explicitly states it is immaterial who offered the provocation.

provision: BNS S. 101 Exception 4 / IPC S. 300 Exception 4
learningObjective: Understand ingredients of sudden fight exception.

question: Under Exception 5 to Section 101 BNS (Section 300 IPC), culpable homicide is not murder when the person whose death is caused:
options: Being above 18 years of age, suffers death or takes the risk of death with his own consent
Being above 12 years of age, gives consent
Consents under intoxication or delirium
Consents to mercy killing by family members
explanation: Exception 5 requires the deceased to be above the age of 18 years and to have given voluntary, informed consent.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; statutory age limit is above 18 years.
optionBreakdown.B: 12 years is the threshold under general exception S. 27 BNS (S. 90 IPC), not Exception 5.
optionBreakdown.C: Consent under delirium or intoxication is invalid.
optionBreakdown.D: Euthanasia is governed by Supreme Court guidelines, not Exception 5.

provision: BNS S. 101 Exception 5 / IPC S. 300 Exception 5
learningObjective: Verify age threshold in Exception 5.

question: Under Proviso 1 to Exception 1, the provocation must NOT be:
options: Sought or voluntarily provoked by the offender as an excuse for killing
Given by anything done in obedience to law
Given by anything done in lawful exercise of private defence
All of the above
explanation: Provisos 1, 2, and 3 to Exception 1 bar provocation that is self-sought, in obedience to law, or in lawful exercise of private defence.

optionBreakdown.A: Barred under Proviso 1.
optionBreakdown.B: Barred under Proviso 2.
optionBreakdown.D: Correct; all three provisos negate Exception 1.

provision: BNS S. 101 Exception 1 Provisos / IPC S. 300 Provisos
learningObjective: Master provisos to Grave & Sudden Provocation.

question: What is the statutory punishment for Culpable Homicide Not Amounting to Murder with intention under Section 105 Part I BNS (IPC S. 304 Part I)?
options: Imprisonment for life or imprisonment up to 10 years and fine
Rigorous imprisonment up to 5 years only
Simple imprisonment up to 3 years
Capital punishment
explanation: Section 105 Part I BNS (IPC S. 304 Part I) prescribes life imprisonment or imprisonment of either description up to 10 years, and fine.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; life imprisonment or imprisonment up to 10 years and fine.
optionBreakdown.B: Incorrect penalty.
optionBreakdown.D: Death penalty is not available for culpable homicide not amounting to murder.

provision: BNS S. 105 / IPC S. 304 Part I
learningObjective: Understand punishment for culpable homicide.

question: If an act is done with knowledge that it is likely to cause death, but without any intention to cause death, under which part of Section 105 BNS (S. 304 IPC) is it punished?
options: Part I
Part II
Section 103
Section 106
explanation: Part II of S. 105 BNS (S. 304 IPC) punishes culpable homicide committed with knowledge but without intention (up to 10 years, or fine, or both).

optionBreakdown.A: Part I applies where there is intention to cause death or grievous injury.
optionBreakdown.B: Correct; Part II applies to knowledge without intention.

provision: BNS S. 105 / IPC S. 304 Part II
learningObjective: Differentiate S. 304 Part I vs Part II.

question: In which case did the Supreme Court hold that the words 'sudden fight' imply mutual combat where blows are exchanged on both sides?
options: Ghapoo Yadav v. State of M.P. (2003)
Dudh Nath Pandey v. State of U.P. (1981)
Kehar Singh v. State (1988)
State of A.P. v. Rayavarapu Punnayya (1977)
explanation: In Ghapoo Yadav v. State of M.P. (2003), the Supreme Court detailed the four elements of Exception 4 including bilateral mutual combat.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; Ghapoo Yadav clarifies Exception 4.
optionBreakdown.B: Deals with plea of alibi.
optionBreakdown.D: Deals with distinction between S. 299 and S. 300.

provision: BNS S. 101 Exception 4 / IPC S. 300 Exception 4
learningObjective: Analyze case law on Exception 4.

question: Exception 3 to Section 101 BNS (Section 300 IPC) protects a public servant who causes death, provided:
options: He acts in good faith, believing his act to be lawful and necessary for the due discharge of his duty, without ill-will
He had an explicit shoot-to-kill executive order
The victim was an accused felon regardless of offence severity
The act was committed during election duty
explanation: Exception 3 requires good faith, lawful discharge of public duty, and absence of personal ill-will towards the person killed.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; statutory wording of Exception 3.
optionBreakdown.B: Orders do not justify intentional murder outside necessity.
optionBreakdown.C: No general right to execute felons.
optionBreakdown.D: Duty must satisfy statutory good faith.

provision: BNS S. 101 Exception 3 / IPC S. 300 Exception 3
learningObjective: Understand public servant exception.

question: What is the statutory punishment under Section 106(1) BNS for causing death by any rash or negligent act not amounting to culpable homicide (general category)?
options: Imprisonment up to 2 years, or fine, or both
Imprisonment up to 5 years, and shall also be liable to fine
Imprisonment up to 7 years
Imprisonment up to 10 years
explanation: Section 106(1) BNS increased the general penalty for causing death by rash/negligent act from 2 years (under IPC S. 304A) to imprisonment up to 5 years and fine.

optionBreakdown.A: This was the penalty under IPC Section 304A.
optionBreakdown.B: Correct; BNS Section 106(1) provides up to 5 years and fine.
optionBreakdown.D: 10 years is under subsection (2) which is currently held in abeyance.

learningObjective: Master S. 106(1) general punishment.

question: Under the Proviso to Section 106(1) BNS, if a registered medical practitioner causes death while performing a medical procedure, what is the maximum imprisonment?
options: Up to 1 year, or fine, or both
Up to 2 years, and fine
Up to 5 years
Complete statutory immunity from criminal prosecution
explanation: The Proviso to Section 106(1) BNS caps punishment for registered medical practitioners at imprisonment up to 2 years and fine.

optionBreakdown.A: Incorrect period.
optionBreakdown.B: Correct; proviso limits medical negligence imprisonment to 2 years.
optionBreakdown.C: 5 years is the general penalty for non-medical offenders.
optionBreakdown.D: Doctors do not have absolute immunity under S. 106(1).

learningObjective: Recognize special medical practitioner proviso under S. 106(1).

question: What is the status of Section 106(2) BNS (enhanced 10-year punishment for hit-and-run without reporting) as per MHA Notification S.O. 850(E)?
options: Fully in force from 1 July 2024
Struck down by the Supreme Court as unconstitutional
Excluded from enforcement and held in abeyance pending consultation
Repealed by the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam
explanation: MHA Gazette Notification S.O. 850(E) dated 23 Feb 2024 brought BNS into force on 1 July 2024 EXCEPT sub-section (2) of Section 106.

optionBreakdown.A: Incorrect; S. 106(2) was explicitly omitted from the commencement notification.
optionBreakdown.B: Not struck down by judiciary; held back by executive notification.
optionBreakdown.C: Correct; held in abeyance pending consultations with transport associations.
optionBreakdown.D: Not repealed; enacted by Parliament but commencement deferred.

learningObjective: Understand crucial S. 106(2) stay caveat.

question: In which landmark case did the Supreme Court lay down guidelines for prosecuting medical professionals for criminal negligence under IPC S. 304A (now BNS S. 106)?
options: Jacob Mathew v. State of Punjab (2005)
Common Cause v. Union of India (2018)
Aruna Shanbaug v. Union of India (2011)
Parmanand Katara v. Union of India (1989)
explanation: Jacob Mathew v. State of Punjab ((2005) 6 SCC 1) established that medical negligence requires gross lack of competence or care (Bolam test adapted to criminal law).

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; Jacob Mathew is the leading authority on medical criminal negligence.
optionBreakdown.B: Deals with passive euthanasia and living will.
optionBreakdown.D: Deals with duty of doctors to provide immediate emergency care.

learningObjective: Recall Jacob Mathew ruling.

question: To attract Section 106(1) BNS (Section 304A IPC), the death must be the direct result of the rash or negligent act, known in law as:
options: Causa causans (immediate direct cause)
Causa sine qua non (remote cause)
Res ipsa loquitur
Volenti non fit injuria
explanation: Under Emperor v. Omkar Rampratap and reaffirmed in Kurban Hussein (1965), death must be the causa causans (direct, immediate, proximate cause).

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; causa causans is required.
optionBreakdown.B: Causa sine qua non is insufficient for criminal liability.
optionBreakdown.C: Rule of civil evidence, not the test of proximate causation.

learningObjective: Master causa causans causation doctrine.

question: Can Section 106(1) BNS (Section 304A IPC) apply where the accused had the intention to cause death?
options: Yes, always
No; Section 106 applies only where there is NEITHER intention NOR knowledge that the act will cause death
Yes, provided the weapon was not deadly
Only if the victim was a trespasser
explanation: Section 106(1) explicitly states 'causes death of any person by doing any rash or negligent act not amounting to culpable homicide'. Where intention or knowledge exists, it falls under S. 100/101/105.

optionBreakdown.A: Incorrect; intention excludes Section 106.
optionBreakdown.B: Correct; Section 106 applies only where culpable homicide is ruled out.

learningObjective: Distinguish S. 106 from culpable homicide.

question: What is the difference between 'rashness' and 'negligence' in criminal jurisprudence?
options: Rashness implies acting with consciousness of the risk; negligence implies breach of duty to take care through inadvertence or indifference
Rashness is an intentional offence; negligence is accidental
Rashness applies only to vehicles; negligence applies only to doctors
There is no legal difference between them
explanation: As explained in Niranjan Singh and Bhalchandra, rashness involves acting despite foreseeing the dangerous risk; negligence is omitting to do what a prudent person would do.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; classical distinction between rashness and negligence.
optionBreakdown.B: Neither involves intention to cause death.

learningObjective: Differentiate criminal rashness from negligence.

question: If brought into force, what sentence does Section 106(2) BNS prescribe for a driver who escapes without reporting the accident to police or magistrate?
options: Imprisonment up to 3 years and fine
Imprisonment up to 7 years and fine
Imprisonment up to 10 years, and shall also be liable to fine
Life imprisonment
explanation: Section 106(2) provides imprisonment up to 10 years and fine for escaping without reporting soon after the incident.

optionBreakdown.A: Incorrect.
optionBreakdown.B: Incorrect.
optionBreakdown.C: Correct; S. 106(2) provides up to 10 years.

learningObjective: Recall proposed penalty under S. 106(2).

question: In Cherubin Gregory v. State of Bihar (1964), the accused fixed live electric wires to his latrine to deter trespassers, resulting in the death of a trespasser. He was held guilty under:
options: Section 304A IPC (now BNS S. 106(1))
Section 300 IPC (Murder)
Section 323 IPC (Simple Hurt)
Not guilty under right of private defence of property
explanation: In Cherubin Gregory v. State of Bihar (AIR 1964 SC 205), setting uninsulated live wires was held to be a rash and negligent act causing death under S. 304A.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; convicted under S. 304A.
optionBreakdown.B: Not held guilty of murder.
optionBreakdown.C: Death resulted, so not simple hurt.
optionBreakdown.D: Private defence does not permit setting lethal man-traps without warning.

learningObjective: Analyze Cherubin Gregory man-trap precedent.

question: What is the equivalent of Section 304A IPC in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023?
options: Section 103
Section 105
Section 106
Section 115
explanation: Section 304A IPC corresponds to Section 106 BNS.

optionBreakdown.A: Section 103 BNS corresponds to Section 302 IPC (Murder).
optionBreakdown.B: Section 105 BNS corresponds to Section 304 IPC (Culpable Homicide).
optionBreakdown.C: Correct; Section 106 BNS corresponds to Section 304A IPC.
optionBreakdown.D: Section 115 BNS corresponds to Section 323 IPC (Hurt).

learningObjective: Map statutory section numbers for rash death.

question: Under Section 79 BNS (Section 304B IPC), what is the statutory time frame within which the unnatural death of a woman must occur for dowry death?
options: Within 3 years of marriage
Within 5 years of marriage
Within 7 years of marriage
Within 10 years of marriage
explanation: Section 79 BNS (and Section 304B IPC) specifies death occurring within 7 years of marriage.

optionBreakdown.A: Incorrect.
optionBreakdown.B: Incorrect.
optionBreakdown.C: Correct; statutory period is within 7 years of marriage.

learningObjective: Recall time threshold for dowry death.

question: What is the minimum statutory punishment for Dowry Death under Section 79 BNS (Section 304B IPC)?
options: Imprisonment for 3 years
Imprisonment for 5 years
Imprisonment for 7 years
Imprisonment for 10 years
explanation: The minimum sentence for dowry death is imprisonment for 7 years, which may extend to imprisonment for life.

optionBreakdown.A: Too low.
optionBreakdown.B: Too low.
optionBreakdown.D: Maximum may be life, but minimum is 7 years.

learningObjective: Identify minimum punishment for dowry death.

question: Which provision of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 specifically introduces murder by a mob of five or more persons on grounds of race, caste, community, sex, or place of birth (Mob Lynching)?
options: Section 103(1)
Section 103(2)
Section 111(2)
Section 189
explanation: Section 103(2) BNS is a groundbreaking new provision punishing murder committed by 5 or more persons acting in concert on grounds of race, caste, community, sex, place of birth, language, or religion with death or life imprisonment.

optionBreakdown.A: Section 103(1) is the general penalty for murder.
optionBreakdown.B: Correct; Section 103(2) BNS covers mob lynching.

learningObjective: Master new Mob Lynching provision in BNS S. 103(2).

question: What is the statutory punishment prescribed under Section 103(2) BNS for mob lynching?
options: Rigorous imprisonment for 7 years
Imprisonment for 10 years and fine
Death or imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine
Imprisonment up to 14 years
explanation: Section 103(2) BNS prescribes death or imprisonment for life, and fine, for each member of such group.

optionBreakdown.A: Incorrect penalty.
optionBreakdown.B: Incorrect penalty.

learningObjective: Understand mob lynching penalties.

question: Under Section 108 BNS (Section 306 IPC), what is the maximum punishment for Abetment of Suicide?
options: Imprisonment up to 5 years
Imprisonment up to 7 years
Imprisonment up to 10 years, and fine
Life imprisonment
explanation: Section 108 BNS (S. 306 IPC) punishes abetment of suicide with imprisonment of either description for a term up to 10 years, and fine.

optionBreakdown.A: Incorrect.
optionBreakdown.B: Incorrect.
optionBreakdown.C: Correct; up to 10 years and fine.
optionBreakdown.D: Life imprisonment applies if suicide is abetted of a child or insane person (S. 107 BNS / S. 305 IPC).

learningObjective: Recall punishment for abetment of suicide.

question: Section 107 BNS (Section 305 IPC) deals with abetment of suicide of:
options: Any child under 18 years, insane person, or intoxicated person
A public servant
A married woman within 7 years of marriage
An army officer on active duty
explanation: Section 107 BNS punishes abetment of suicide of any person under 18 years of age, insane, delirious, or intoxicated with death or life imprisonment, or up to 10 years.

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; statutory protected categories in S. 107 BNS / S. 305 IPC.
optionBreakdown.B: Not a distinct section.
optionBreakdown.C: Falls under S. 108 BNS with presumption under S. 117 BSA (S. 113A IEA).

learningObjective: Differentiate S. 107 from S. 108 BNS.

question: Which essential ingredient must be established for dowry death under S. 79 BNS (S. 304B IPC)?
options: Cruelty or harassment by husband or his relatives was 'soon before her death' in connection with demand for dowry
Husband was physically present at the scene of death
Demand for dowry was made in writing before solemnisation
The marriage was an inter-caste marriage
explanation: The phrase 'soon before her death' establishes proximate and live link between cruelty for dowry and the unnatural death (Satvir Singh v. State of Punjab).

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; 'soon before her death' is the crucial proximate link.
optionBreakdown.B: Physical presence of husband at moment of death is not required.

learningObjective: Understand 'soon before her death' requirement.

question: In which case did the Supreme Court hold that to convict under S. 306 IPC for abetment of suicide, there must be clear mens rea, active instigation or direct act leading the deceased to commit suicide?
options: Sanju alias Sanjay Singh Sengar v. State of M.P. (2002)
State of West Bengal v. Orilal Jaiswal (1994)
Ramesh Kumar v. State of Chhattisgarh (2001)
All of the above
explanation: A long line of judgments including Sanju Sengar, Orilal Jaiswal, and Ramesh Kumar established that mere harassment or abusive words without active instigation does not constitute abetment under S. 306.

optionBreakdown.A: Leading case on word 'go and die'.
optionBreakdown.B: Leading case on high proof standard for abetment.
optionBreakdown.D: Correct; all three reinforce this consistent jurisprudence.

learningObjective: Analyze mens rea requirement in abetment of suicide.

question: How did BNS 2023 treat Attempt to Commit Suicide (formerly Section 309 IPC)?
options: Retained identically with 1 year simple imprisonment
Shifted to Section 226 BNS, punishing attempt to commit suicide to compel or restrain exercise of lawful power
Abolished entirely with no offence remaining in the penal code
Made punishable with capital punishment
explanation: Section 309 IPC is replaced by Section 226 BNS, which punishes attempting suicide ONLY with intent to compel/restrain a public servant from discharging duty (with up to 1 year, fine, or community service).

optionBreakdown.A: General suicide attempt was not retained identically.
optionBreakdown.B: Correct; S. 226 BNS covers attempt to commit suicide to compel/restrain lawful power.
optionBreakdown.C: A restricted form is retained in S. 226.

learningObjective: Recognize reform of attempt to commit suicide in BNS.

question: In Tehseen S. Poonawalla v. Union of India (2018), what did the Supreme Court mandate regarding mob lynching?
options: Parliament should create a separate offence for lynching, and States must take preventive, remedial and punitive measures
Mob lynching is an internal security matter beyond judicial review
All participants should be tried under military court martials
Sections 141-149 IPC are unconstitutional
explanation: Tehseen Poonawalla ((2018) 9 SCC 501) issued comprehensive guidelines and recommended enactment of a standalone lynching law, which influenced BNS S. 103(2).

optionBreakdown.A: Correct; Tehseen Poonawalla guidelines prompted specific statutory provisions.
optionBreakdown.B: Incorrect.

learningObjective: Trace constitutional origin of BNS mob lynching law.

question: Under Section 114 BNS (Section 319 IPC), Hurt is defined as causing:
options: Bodily pain, disease or infirmity to any person
Mental agony or emotional distress
Damage to clothes or property
Loss of reputation or standing
explanation: Hurt is defined as causing bodily pain, disease or infirmity to any person.

optionBreakdown.B: Mental pain alone does not constitute bodily hurt under this section.

learningObjective: Define simple hurt.

question: How many statutory clauses designate 'Grievous Hurt' under Section 116 BNS (Section 320 IPC)?
options: Five clauses
Six clauses
Eight clauses
Ten clauses
explanation: Both IPC Section 320 and BNS Section 116 specify exactly eight designated kinds of hurt as grievous hurt.

optionBreakdown.A: Incorrect.
optionBreakdown.B: Incorrect.
optionBreakdown.C: Correct; eight clauses designate grievous hurt.

learningObjective: Recall eight clauses of grievous hurt.

question: Under Clause Eighth of Section 116 BNS (Section 320 IPC), any hurt which causes the sufferer to be during what space of time in severe bodily pain, or unable to follow his ordinary pursuits, is grievous hurt?
options: 14 days
20 days
30 days
40 days
explanation: Clause Eighth specifies a period of 20 days during which the victim is in severe bodily pain or unable to follow ordinary pursuits.

optionBreakdown.A: Incorrect.

provision: BNS S. 116 Clause 8 / IPC S. 320 Clause 8
learningObjective: Verify 20-day rule for grievous hurt.

question: Which of the following is NOT one of the eight clauses of Grievous Hurt under Section 116 BNS (Section 320 IPC)?

Permanent privation of the sight of either eye
Simple contusion causing pain for 7 days
Fracture or dislocation of a bone or tooth
explanation: Simple contusion causing pain for only 7 days falls under simple hurt; only hurt causing severe pain/inability for 20 days becomes grievous under Clause 8.

optionBreakdown.A: Clause 1.
optionBreakdown.B: Clause 2.

learningObjective: Distinguish simple hurt from grievous hurt.

question: What is the statutory punishment for voluntarily causing grievous hurt by use of acid under Section 124(1) BNS (Section 326A IPC)?
options: Imprisonment of not less than 5 years up to 10 years
Imprisonment of not less than 10 years which may extend to life imprisonment, and fine
Imprisonment up to 7 years
Imprisonment for 3 years only
explanation: Section 124(1) BNS (IPC S. 326A) provides mandatory minimum imprisonment of 10 years, up to life, with fine to cover medical expenses.

optionBreakdown.A: Too lenient.
optionBreakdown.B: Correct; minimum 10 years up to life, and fine payable to victim.
